questions.question: A company runs a monolithic application on EC2 behind a Classic Load Balancer. The team now wants to split the application into microservices and route requests so that example.com/users goes to one service and example.com/posts goes to another, using a single load balancer. What should they do?
options: Keep the Classic Load Balancer and add listeners for each URL path
Replace it with an Application Load Balancer using path-based routing to separate target groups
Replace it with a Network Load Balancer and use TCP rules to split the paths
Replace it with a Gateway Load Balancer and route the paths to virtual appliances
questions.explanation: An ALB supports routing rules based on the path in the URL, sending each path to its own target group, so one ALB replaces multiple CLBs. Keeping the CLB fails because a CLB cannot do path-based routing and would need one load balancer per application. An NLB forwards TCP/UDP only and is not HTTP-path-aware. A GWLB operates at Layer 3 to insert appliances, not to route application URLs.

questions.question: A web application runs on EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The application must log the real public IP address of each visitor for fraud analysis, but the servers currently record only a private 10.x address. What is the correct explanation and fix?
options: The load balancer terminates the connection, so the client IP is available in the X-Forwarded-For header
The security group is masking the source address, so allow inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0
The instances need public IPs so that the client address is preserved in the packet header
The ALB should be replaced by a Classic Load Balancer, which passes the client IP in the packet
questions.explanation: Because the ALB terminates the client connection, backends see the load balancer's private IP; the ALB inserts the true client IP in X-Forwarded-For (with X-Forwarded-Port and X-Forwarded-Proto for port and protocol). Security groups do not rewrite source IPs, so allowing 0.0.0.0/0 changes nothing. Public IPs on instances do not restore the client address. A CLB also terminates connections and does not solve this.

questions.question: A trading platform must accept both TCP and UDP traffic, sustain millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency, and give each partner a fixed address to whitelist per Availability Zone. Which load balancer type meets these requirements?
options: Classic Load Balancer with HTTP and TCP listeners
Application Load Balancer with host-based routing rules
Network Load Balancer with a static IP per AZ and Elastic IPs
Gateway Load Balancer with GENEVE encapsulation
questions.explanation: The NLB is the Layer 4 load balancer for TCP and UDP at millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency, and it provides one static IP per AZ with Elastic IP support for whitelisting. A CLB supports TCP but not UDP and offers no static per-AZ IPs. An ALB is Layer 7 HTTP only. A GWLB is Layer 3 for third-party appliances, not application traffic balancing.

questions.question: A solutions architect wants a single entry point with static IP addresses for external partners, but the backend services still need HTTP routing by hostname and path. Which design achieves this?
options: An Application Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses attached to its nodes
A Gateway Load Balancer in front of an Application Load Balancer target group
An Application Load Balancer with IP-address target groups pointing to partner networks
A Network Load Balancer with an Application Load Balancer as its target group
questions.explanation: An NLB target group can contain an ALB, giving static IPs for whitelisting in front of Layer 7 routing. An ALB does not offer static per-AZ IP assignment, so attaching Elastic IPs to it is not the described option. A GWLB is for Layer 3 appliance insertion, not application routing. ALB IP target groups must be private IPs and do not provide the static front-end IPs.

questions.question: A security team must insert third-party firewall and intrusion-prevention virtual appliances transparently into all traffic entering and leaving a VPC, scaling the appliance fleet as needed. Which load balancer should be used?
options: Gateway Load Balancer, operating at Layer 3 on IP packets
Network Load Balancer, operating at Layer 4 on TCP and UDP
Application Load Balancer, operating at Layer 7 on HTTP requests
Classic Load Balancer, operating at Layer 4 and Layer 7
questions.explanation: The GWLB deploys, scales and manages fleets of third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls, IDS/IPS and deep packet inspection systems, operating at Layer 3 on IP packets. The NLB balances TCP/UDP application traffic and does not insert appliances into the path. The ALB balances HTTP requests. A CLB is a legacy application balancer and has no appliance-insertion role.

questions.question: Which statement about the encapsulation used by Gateway Load Balancer is correct?
options: It uses GRE on port 4789 to tunnel IP packets to the appliances
It uses GENEVE on port 6081 to send traffic to the virtual appliances
It uses VXLAN on port 8472 to send traffic to the virtual appliances
It uses TLS on port 443 to send HTTP requests to the virtual appliances
questions.explanation: The GWLB uses the GENEVE protocol on port 6081 to send traffic to the appliances. GRE, VXLAN and TLS are not the GWLB encapsulation described in the source, and TLS on 443 is an application-layer protocol inconsistent with Layer 3 packet handling.

questions.question: An application runs as many Docker containers on Amazon ECS, each exposing a different dynamic host port on the same EC2 instance. The team wants one load balancer to route to all of these containers. Which capability makes this possible?
options: Classic Load Balancer with one listener per container port
Network Load Balancer with static IPs per Availability Zone
Application Load Balancer port mapping to dynamic ports in ECS
Gateway Load Balancer with GENEVE on port 6081
questions.explanation: The ALB's port mapping feature redirects to a dynamic port in ECS, so one ALB can serve many container tasks on the same machine. A CLB would require one load balancer per application. An NLB is Layer 4 and does not provide the ECS dynamic port mapping described here. A GWLB is for Layer 3 appliance insertion, not container routing.
questions.keyTopic: ALB target groups (EC2, ECS, Lambda, IPs)

questions.question: A team wants requests for a mobile client to reach an EC2-based target group and requests from desktop clients to reach an on-premises service reachable by private IP, all through one load balancer. The clients include the value ?Platform=Mobile or ?Platform=Desktop in each request. Which configuration fits?
options: An Application Load Balancer with query string routing rules to two target groups
A Network Load Balancer with TCP listener rules that inspect the query string
A Classic Load Balancer with two listeners distinguished by the query string
A Gateway Load Balancer that forwards query strings to virtual appliances
questions.explanation: An ALB can route on query string parameters, sending ?Platform=Mobile to one target group and ?Platform=Desktop to another, and ALB IP target groups can be private on-premises IPs. An NLB operates at Layer 4 and does not inspect query strings. A CLB cannot route on query strings. A GWLB works on IP packets for appliances, not on HTTP query strings.
questions.keyTopic: ALB query string and header routing

questions.question: Which statement about health checks and supported target types across the load balancer types is correct?
options: An NLB can only perform TCP health checks because it forwards only TCP traffic
An ALB configures health checks per load balancer, applying the same check to all target groups
An NLB supports TCP, HTTP and HTTPS health checks, and an ALB configures health checks at the target group level
A Gateway Load Balancer can register a public IP address as a target for its appliances
questions.explanation: NLB health checks support TCP, HTTP and HTTPS, and ALB health checks are configured at the target group level so different groups can be checked independently. The claim that an NLB only performs TCP checks is a common misconception. ALB checks are per target group, not per load balancer. GWLB IP targets must be private IPs, not public.
